title: Timothy Boomer Captures the Uncanny World of Insect Galls
description: Gall wasps, also known as cynipids, have a unique mutual relationship with plants. Their name is derived from the deposits, called galls, which th
body:
Gall wasps, also known as cynipids, have a unique mutual relationship with plants. Their name is derived from the deposits, called galls, which they induce on host plants to support their larvae. The benign growths are created by chemicals that the larvae insert into the plant, drawing on its resources. These phenomena are often very tiny, occasionally appear in clusters, and can range from ruddy brown to vibrant pinks and yellows. Nature photographer Timothy Boomer can’t get enough of them.
“Galls can be brought about by many different organisms, but I tend to focus on the ones induced by cynipid wasps because they are the most visually stunning (at least in my opinion),” Boomer tells Colossal.
Striped volcano gall induced by the cynipid wasp (Feron atrimentum, formerly Andricus atrimentus), Solano County, California
A gall serves as both protection and a food source for the insect growing inside. If all goes according to plan, the larva remains safe from predators, receives enough food, and grows into an adult before climbing out and continuing the cycle. Different species of wasp create unique characteristics, often on very specific parts of the plants. Scientists believe there are at least around 1,300 cynipids globally.
Sometimes, environmental effects change the nodules’ appearance. Boomer points to the spined turban gall, which typically has a bubblegum-pink hue with spines protruding from a relatively flat center. He also captured an atypical one, which is a darker pink with blackened tips and spikes all over. “In this case, normal development was interrupted by a non-inducer entering the gall at an early stage,” Boomer says. “I’m not a scientist, so I won’t pretend to fully comprehend the intricacies of how all this plays out, but I think of it as a ‘home invasion’ that actually alters the home.”
At such minuscule scale with shallow depth-of-field, Boomer uses a focus-stacking technique, which involves taking hundreds, sometimes thousands of images and layering them digitally to make the tiny objects clear. He edits minimally in Photoshop to retain the integrity of the original scene and is passionate about sharing only what occurs naturally. Essentially, he lets the beautiful, bizarre geometries be what they are. “Nature does not need to be ‘enhanced,'” he says.
Find Boomer’s work on Instagram, where you can explore slime molds, flowers, and more.
Urchin gall wasp (Antron quercusechinus), gall on blue oak, Lake Berryessa, Napa County, California
Spined turban gall wasp (Antron douglasii) on valley oak, Solano County, California, USA
Flange gall induced by undescribed Cynipid wasp on blue oak, Vacaville, Solano County, California
Disc gall wasp (Feron parmula), extreme close-up of the surface of a single gall, Lake Berryessa, Napa County, California
Beaked twig gall induced by Burnettweldia plumbella (formerly Disholcaspis plumbella), Lake Berryessa, Napa County, California
Red cone galls induced by Feron kingi on a valley oak leaf, Vacaville, Solano County, California, USA.

title: Pipo Nguyen-duy, Beloved Photography Professor, Murdered at 64
description:
Obituary
                "He took a lot of joy in his everyday life. He sought to make really beautiful photos, and strove to ma
body:
Obituary
                "He took a lot of joy in his everyday life. He sought to make really beautiful photos, and strove to make the world a more beautiful place," said his former student.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Pipo Nguyen-duy was a photography professor and the chair of the studio art department at Oberlin College in Ohio. (image courtesy Oberlin College)
    
        
            Pipo Nguyen-duy, a beloved 64-year-old photography professor and the studio art department chair at Oberlin College in Ohio, and his wife, 56-year-old Tran Thi Phong, were fatally shot in their home on Wednesday, October 28. Nguyen-duy's child and Phong's stepchild, 31-year-old Asia Nguyen-duy (birthname Daniel Jones), has been charged with their deaths and faces six counts of murder, one count of tampering with evidence, and four counts of felonious assault, per Oberlin Municipal Court records. "I am deeply concerned about the impact of the devastating loss of Pipo to our community," Oberlin President Carmen Twillie Ambar wrote in a statement. "Pipo was beloved. During his years at Oberlin, he touched all of us through his passion for photography."Pipo Nguyen-duy, "Mercury” (1995–98 / 2025) (image courtesy CLAMP)

title: 10 Years Later, Magenta Plains Is Still Embracing the Unexpected
description:
Features
                An anniversary exhibition spotlights the artists who’ve made the gallery one of Lower Manhattan’s most
body:
Features
                An anniversary exhibition spotlights the artists who’ve made the gallery one of Lower Manhattan’s most adventurous success stories.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Left to right: Olivia Smith, David Deutsch, and Chris Dorland (photo Don Stahl, courtesy Magenta Plains)
    
        
            Olivia Smith had a thriving career running Exhibition A on the Upper East Side, a company that sells original contemporary art editions, when artists Chris Dorland and David Deutsch approached her in 2015 about opening a gallery on the Lower East Side.Smith had worked with hundreds of artists producing limited edition prints, but she had never managed a commercial gallery or negotiated with museums before. Still, she felt a kinship with Dorland and Deutsch, who found a ground-floor storefront on Allen Street and needed help programming it. First they had to agree on a name, as long as it wasn’t their own on the door.“We wanted something expansive and open-ended,” Smith told Hyperallergic. “We felt Magenta Plains represented a place, but we didn’t know what that place was that we were building yet.”Magenta Plains's building at 149 Canal Street (photo Aaron Short/Hyperallergic)A decade later, Magenta Plains has helped define what the Downtown contemporary art scene can offer the world. The gallery, which outgrew its original location and currently occupies a 4,500-square-foot space at 149 Canal Street, has featured groundbreaking technology-influenced installations, sculptures, and paintings, selections of which are on display in its 10 Year Anniversary show, up through October 31.

title: MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Announce Novel Collection Alliance
description:
News
                The partnership between the museums will include intermuseum loans and joint exhibitions.
body:
News
                The partnership between the museums will include intermuseum loans and joint exhibitions.  
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            From left to right: Museum of Modern Art director Christophe Cherix, M+ Museum Director Suhanya Raffel, and Centre Pompidou President Laurent Le Bon (photo © Centre Pompidou/Chau-Cuong Lê)Leaders at Manhattan's Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), Paris's Centre Pompidou, and M+ in Hong Kong signed an agreement granting unprecedented access to each museum's holdings for increased viewership, more collaborative curation, and additional research. The alliance emerges on the eve of M+'s fifth anniversary at its physical location in Hong Kong's West Kowloon Cultural District, and just one year into MoMA director Christophe Cherix's tenure. The agreement follows a wave of institutional resource pooling and joint acquisitions that swelled in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic as museums seek to reduce overhead costs while navigating major deficits. In another shakeup earlier this year, the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced its forthcoming merger with Ronald Lauder's Neue Galerie, which is set to commence in 2028.“Museums must evolve to reflect the complexity of our world,” said M+ Museum Director Suhanya Raffel in a press statement on the alliance. An exterior view of M+ overlooking Victoria Harbor from Hong Kong's Kowloon peninsula (photo Joe Wong, courtesy M+, Hong Kong)Previous collaborations between M+, home to the Sigg collection of contemporary Chinese art among thousands of other contemporary works from across Asia, and the other two museums foregrounded this agreement. The Hong Kong-based museum signed a memorandum of understanding with the MoMA in early 2025 that established shared curatorial, conservation, and scholarship objectives. And this spring, M+ and Centre Pompidou entered a strategic partnership to “strengthen the cultural dialogue” between their respective continents through joint exhibitions, collections sharing, and a funded fellowship.

title: The Greatest Art Costumes From Hyperallergic's Halloween Party
description: A Dutch still life, “Beast Jesus,” several esoteric Goya characters, and not one but two Marina Abramović/Ulay references (and not even t
body:
A Dutch still life, “Beast Jesus,” several esoteric Goya characters, and not one but two Marina Abramović/Ulay references (and not even the most obvious ones!) walk into a bar ... That’s a Hyperallergic Halloween, baby! On Wednesday evening, October 28, almost 200 of our members, readers, artists, supporters, and their enthusiastic friends rolled into Oberon in Brooklyn for our annual art costume party. Winners in several categories ranging from “Best in Show” to “Most Likely to Get Censored in Florida” brought out the art-history nerd within them, materializing into both immediately recognizable icons — Roy Lichtenstein's “Drowning Girls” and Johannes Vermeer’s “Girl with a Pearl Earring” — and admirably obscure references (oh, she was an Eva Hesse rope sculpture?!).We’re so grateful to our absurdly smart, creative, and crafty community for their commitment to the bit. And a big shout-out to Zac Thompson for their incredible photographs, which will help us relive the night for many moons, or at least as we wait impatiently for next year ... 🌝Best in ShowBest in Show winners Emilio Rojas and Chico Raro as Pedro Lemebel and Francisco Casa Silva of Las Yeguas del Apocalipsis’s “Las Dos Fridas” (1989). No bribing was necessary to convince the panel.  Most EsotericZoë Lescaze and Michael Rossi made every part of their costumes from scratch — yes, including the chair — to dress as lesser-known characters from Francisco Goya's Los caprichos (1797–98) series. The couple was among the winners of the "Most Esoteric" award, naturally.Most Likely to Get Censored in FloridaRichard Prince's "Wayward Nurse" (2005), part of the artist's series critiquing the sexualization of nurses on pulp-fiction book covers, would not fly in the Sunshine State in 2026!Most Likely to Get Acquired by a Museum UnironicallyCurators and staff from the Heckscher Museum of Art in Huntington, New York, recreated a painting from the institution's own collection: George Grosz's antifascist "Eclipse of the Sun" (1926).People's ChoiceMelissa Brown and Marie Lorenz won over the crowd as none other than the infamously botched “Ecce Homo” aka “Beast Jesus” and its author, restorer Cecilia Giménez Zueco!Hyperallergic Co-founders Veken Gueyikian and Hrag Vartanian with one of this year's costume contest judges, Nicholas D. Lowry, president of Swann Auction Galleries. Veken is Kazimir Malevich’s “Black Square” (1915), and Vartanian is a 17th-century Dutch still life painting — check out the skull! (Memento mori, very Halloween-coded.)Our wonderful costume contest judges! Left to right: New York Democratic Congressional candidate Claire Valdez, artist Jia Sung as the Spirit of Spirit Airlines (aka what everyone used to take to get to Art Basel Miami Beach), critic Aruna D’Souza in sleek black feathers, and Nicholas D. Lowry as a fashionable pumpkin in plaid.Hyperallergic Staff Writer Anna Lee as Johannes Vermeer’s “Girl with a Pearl Earring” (c. 1665) — an art-history classic, made otherworldly by photographer Zac Thompson’s expert double exposure.These guests brought Museo del Prado right to your doorstep as a rather gory version of Francisco Goya's “Saturn Devouring His Son” (1820–23). Body horror!Artist Coco Fusco donned one of the fabulous works in Marisol's wearable wooden sculpture "Three Women with Umbrella" (1965–66). Who says Pop art is dead?If we had a “Cutest” category this year, this pawesome group would have taken the gold! Left to right: Will Swanson, Dwai, Cosette Patterson, Lauren Blaser, Shelby Roller, Sophia Tedesco, and Daniela Alonso as Cassius Marcellus Coolidge’s “A Friend in Need” (1903). Emily Dotsikas of Alma Communications as Roy Lichtenstein’s “Drawing Girl” (1963). Brad, who? Hyperallergic Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara addresses the crowd after a very competitive contest. Just don't ask him what his costume is!Marina Abramović and Ulay’s “Rest Energy” (1980). There’s nothing scarier than a multi-year situationship, except maybe literally putting your heart in the hands of your lover.Hyperallergic Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar went as Snoopy for the fourth year in a row, a costume she calls her “magnum opus.”“I made this Snoopy costume with stuff that I already had at home — the ears, spot, and tail were from an old black tee; I painted an old beauty blender black and used it as Snoopy's nose,” Nayyar shared. “My love of this cartoon beagle is well-known and documented. I'm already a crazy dog lady, but there's something about Snoopy's cheeky attitude and ridiculous antics that flips the script on the ‘man's best friend’ marker, which I find really liberating and inspirational.”Writer Clara Maria Apostolatos (right) and her partner joined forces, quite literally, to embody Marina Abramović and Ulay’s “Relation in Time” (1977). What still life is complete without its peckish butterfly? Houry Geudelekian and Hyperallergic Co-founder and Editor-at-Large Hrag Vartanian make a perfect pair.Us: “What are you?”Artist Danielle De Jesus: “I'm a broke MFA student!”Just brilliant, down to the Whitney Museum artist lifetime pass!Hyperallergic contributors Julie Schneider (middle) as a Keith Haring subway drawing and Daniela Mayer (far right) as an AI girlfriend, with Felix Moody as water and Brian Henderson as Candy Warhol (not pictured: candy corn costume).Artists Jesse Lambert as Ray Johnson and Linda Ganjian as Eva Hesse's rope sculpture "No title" (1970). Is this what they mean by a two-person show?Writer Jennifer Samet of Hyperallergic's beloved “Beer With a Painter” column arrived as the ultimate tastemaker: Peggy Guggenheim.Cheryl Hageman, deputy director of MTA Arts & Design, as a painting from Georgia O'Keeffe's Sky Above Clouds (1960–77) series.

title: To Live Is to Believe
description:
Weekly Newsletter
                Remembering Ursula von Rydingsvard, an Epstein survivor’s message for MoMA, interviews with Pa
body:
Weekly Newsletter
                Remembering Ursula von Rydingsvard, an Epstein survivor’s message for MoMA, interviews with Paul Pfeiffer and Layli Long Soldier, and the best costumes of our artsy Halloween party.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            On a fair afternoon in Queens, New York, a woman in a red dress crosses the street in front of me with an actual axe under her arm. Her face is stern, her step fast, and you can tell from the blood on her axe that she wasn’t using it to chop wood. A police siren wails in the distance, but that doesn’t seem to bother her. I reach to lock the car and then remember it’s Halloween. At a warm and lovely dinner at Cabinet Magazine, founder and editor-in-chief Sina Najafi shows us a photograph of tightrope walker Margret Zimmermann balancing on a high wire above the bombed-out ruins of the Haymarket in Cologne, Germany, in 1946. She looks her finest in her red lipstick, but a treacherous wind is blowing in her hair as a crowd watches from far below.  Outside, Brooklyn seems to be getting richer and poorer at the same time. A man wearing a bejeweled crown asks me for money. In this city, performance artists are beggars and beggars are performance artists. At Hyperallergic’s art-themed Halloween party, dozens of guests show up with impressive costumes and really commit to the act. Claire Valdez, an artist and organizer who’s running for Congress, drops by and serves as a judge in our art costume contest. I don’t have a costume, but I perform all night. “To live is to believe,” Marcel Duchamp says in a video on my phone screen. A little girl dressed as Lady Liberty crosses the street with her mother, a torch in her hand. She keeps the torch held high as they walk off, and that makes me smile.—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

title: Italian Police Used AI to Identify $200 M. Worth of Stolen Art and Antiquities
description: In the fall of 2024, Italian police used AI to analyze photographs taken at a popular antique fair, identifying a particular oil painting as having
body:
In the fall of 2024, Italian police used AI to analyze photographs taken at a popular antique fair, identifying a particular oil painting as having been one stolen from a church near L’Aquila 20 years prior.

	The Carabinieri Command for the Protection of Cultural Heritage, Italy’s art crime squad, has been using an AI algorithm to identify stolen artworks and artifacts since 2023. The platform they use is called SWOADS—or Stolen Works of Art Detection System—and was developed by Salvatore Rapicavoli, an IT engineer who joined the art crime team in 2023.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	A BBC article detailed the process, which began with Italian police officers visiting Mercanteinfiera, a 40-year-old “antiques village” that attracts exhibitors from all over Europe, in October 2024. When the officers uploaded their photographs into the art crime database, Swoads flagged a particular image of a young woman holding a scroll. The oil painting was a close—though, to the human eye, not an exact—match to a 17th-century painting of Saint Agnese that had been taken from Virgo Potens, a small church in Sulmona, in the Abruzzo region. At some point over the past two decades, the lamb Sant Agnese was cradling in the original had been painted over with a scroll inscribed with Latin text. Swoads, however, was able to identify “hidden visual fingerprints in the works—pairing similarities between shades of colour and rough silhouettes.”

	Rapicavoli’s goal of using technology to solve art crime problems has been a success. Swoads has recovered more than 300 large paintings and statues, and more than 165,000 small objects like coins, letters, and medals, according to the BBC. All told, these objects are worth over $200 million. As for the portrait of Saint Agnese, it was returned to the church from where it was stolen. The thieves have yet to be apprehended.
